response.message: We’re building a read-only AWS assistant that finds drift in a synthetic inventory, runs policy checks, drafts a correction plan and a diff for review, and stops at human approval with an audit trail. It never applies or deletes anything. These services aren't covered by the native generators yet, so they're design-only for now. A good first local test is to load a small synthetic inventory with one known drift and check that it gets flagged and the diff shows the fix. In that test the model replies are scripted, so they only prove the plumbing works. Checking that a real Bedrock model writes correct plans needs an approved model ID, account and region. What should we measure drift against: desired-state files you already have (such as Terraform), AWS Config rules, or not sure yet?

proposal.title: First AWS sketch: read-only drift detection and correction proposal
proposal.body: Scope: synthetic inventory snapshot, then policy and drift checks, then plan drafting with Bedrock, then a reviewable diff, then human approval, with an audit trail. Assumptions: there is no path to apply or delete, and credentials are never broadened automatically. Region, account, model ID and policy baseline are still undecided. These services are design-only because no native generator exists for them yet. Local tests use scripted model replies.

request.message:
Act as a patient architecture consultant and teacher. Start with what the evidence shows is working, explain the most important remaining issue in plain language, and help the user make progress. Do not just recite a checklist or demand that a junior developer repair product internals. Offer a concrete supported correction when possible; otherwise ask one focused question and explain why its answer matters. Help improve this architecture from its current emulation results. Diagnose the first actionable finding. Propose a minimal supported architecture correction only when requirements already justify it; otherwise ask one precise question.
Preserve all required components, existing systems, IDs, established service choices, access boundaries and requirements. Never clear unfinished-work gates, remove workload scope, weaken tests or invent successful validation. A graph proposal cannot repair generator/runtime source or an emulator defect: identify that as product engineering work with a reproducer. Model output is not test evidence. A local emulation pass is not a cloud plan or deployment. After an applied correction, rerun emulation on the new artifact; do not reuse this result. response.message:
The good news is that the emulation found no failures. The design is wired end to end and keeps the read-only, no-apply boundary, so the blockers are unfinished work rather than broken logic. The first actionable finding is that the inventory bucket has no explicit access contract, meaning nobody is recorded as allowed to put synthetic snapshots into it. The other seven blockers are missing native implementations for Step Functions, the Lambdas, DynamoDB, CloudTrail and the existing-system references, so those are product engineering work, not diagram fixes.

Who should load the synthetic snapshots and baselines into that bucket: should the platform operator have read and write access to it, or should someone else upload them?
